models.name: Tesla Model 3
models.review: A fully electric sedan offering excellent range and very low running costs. Ideal for buyers who want cutting-edge tech and less maintenance, though it depends on charging infrastructure being available.

models.name: Tesla Model Y
models.review: America's best-selling EV, now with a sharper facelift and a genuinely quick Performance trim option. The RWD version offers the best value in the lineup for buyers who don't need maximum power.

models.name: Tesla Model S
models.review: Tesla's flagship liftback sedan delivers exceptional range and blistering performance, with the Plaid trim rivaling hypercars for straight-line speed. A genuinely quick, tech-laden alternative to German luxury sedans, though cabin material quality still trails rivals like the S-Class.

models.name: Tesla Model X
models.power: 500 kW (670 hp) - base Dual Motor trim
models.review: A quick, spacious luxury electric SUV with distinctive falcon-wing rear doors and genuine three-row capability. The Plaid trim adds supercar-rivaling acceleration, though cabin materials still trail rivals like the BMW iX at this price point.

models.name: Ford Mustang
models.review: A classic American muscle car with genuine V8 power and an iconic engine note. Perfect for enthusiasts of traditional sports-car driving, though fuel consumption is high compared to modern rivals.

models.name: Ford Explorer
models.review: One of the best-driving three-row SUVs in its class, with an available twin-turbo V6 that adds genuine excitement. Strong choice for families who want performance without sacrificing much practicality, though V6 models drink more fuel.

models.name: Ford Escape
models.review: A comfortable compact SUV where the hybrid trim delivers class-leading fuel economy without much compromise in daily usability. A sensible pick for commuters, though the standard turbo engine feels more eager if outright pace matters more than mpg.

models.name: Ford Bronco
models.review: An authentic off-road SUV with removable doors and roof, offering three distinct engine choices up to the fire-breathing 418-hp Raptor. A genuine Wrangler rival that's just as capable off-road while feeling more modern inside.

models.name: Ford Expedition
models.review: A body-on-frame full-size SUV that shares its bones with the F-150, offering genuine towing muscle and eight-passenger seating. The base twin-turbo V6 already feels quick for its size, while the 440-hp High-Output version adds real punch for those who need it.

models.name: Ford Bronco Sport
models.review: A genuinely capable compact off-roader built on the Escape's platform, with standard AWD and trail-focused hardware. The base engine suits daily commuting well, while the 250-hp Badlands trim adds real off-road punch for weekend adventures.

models.name: Ford Mustang Mach-E
models.power: 197 kW (264 hp) - base Select RWD trim
models.review: A genuinely quick electric SUV that borrows the Mustang name and delivers on it, especially in 480-hp GT trim. One of the more affordable ways into a fast, practical EV, with the extended-range RWD trim offering the best range-for-money balance.

models.name: Ford Puma
models.review: Europe's best-selling small SUV combines a genuinely fun-to-drive chassis with efficient mild-hybrid power. Excellent value and practicality in a compact footprint, with the ST version adding real driving thrills.

models.name: Ford Territory
models.review: A value-focused midsize SUV built with JMC for international markets, offering a genuine hybrid option that nearly doubles fuel efficiency over the base EcoBoost. A practical, tech-loaded alternative to the RAV4 and X-Trail in markets where it's sold, though it lacks the badge cachet of Ford's home-market SUVs.

models.name: Ford EVOS
models.review: A China-only coupe-SUV built by Changan Ford, notable for its massive 27-inch dashboard screen and distinctive fastback styling. Renamed Ford Mondeo Sport in 2024 alongside a new 304-hp hybrid powertrain, it has struggled for sales against a flood of domestic Chinese EV rivals.

models.name: Chevrolet Corvette
models.review: An American supercar at a remarkably competitive price against performance that rivals far more expensive European rivals. Excellent value for anyone wanting blistering acceleration and head-turning looks.

models.name: Chevrolet Equinox
models.review: A practical, value-focused compact SUV, now offered alongside a genuinely long-range Equinox EV variant. Best for budget-conscious families who want space and simplicity over outright driving excitement.

models.name: Chevrolet Tahoe
models.review: A full-size family SUV offering a choice of two V8s and a torque-rich Duramax diesel with class-leading highway range. Genuinely spacious and capable for towing, though the base V8's fuel economy trails Ford's turbocharged Expedition.

models.name: Chevrolet Suburban
models.review: The extended-wheelbase sibling to the Tahoe, offering best-in-class cargo volume and up to nine-passenger seating. The Duramax diesel option delivers genuinely impressive highway range up to 728 miles per tank, making it a strong pick for road-trip families.

models.name: Chevrolet Blazer
models.review: Chevrolet's sportiest gas-powered crossover, with the RS trim's optional V6 dropping 0-60 to a genuinely quick 6.1 seconds. Most buyers will find the standard turbo-four sufficiently punchy for daily driving, with a nicely composed ride for the segment.

models.name: Chevrolet Traverse
models.review: A three-row SUV that replaced its old V6 with a single, genuinely strong turbo-four making 328 hp, more than most segment rivals. Spacious and well-equipped, with the off-road Z71 adding twin-clutch AWD for light trail duty.

models.name: Chevrolet Trax
models.review: One of the most affordable new SUVs on sale, offering best-in-class cargo space and surprisingly punchy low-end torque from its small turbo triple. A genuinely smart value pick for budget-conscious buyers who don't need AWD or towing capability.

models.name: Chevrolet Trailblazer
models.review: A value-oriented subcompact SUV with a spacious cabin for its class and strong fuel economy. The optional 1.3-liter engine and AWD combo suits buyers wanting a bit more confidence in bad weather, though acceleration remains modest either way.

models.name: Chevrolet Onix Plus
models.review: A no-frills, affordable hatchback that remains one of Latin America's best-selling cars thanks to low running costs and Chevrolet's wide service network. Not exciting, but hard to beat on value for budget-conscious buyers.

models.name: Chevrolet Onix
models.review: A no-frills, affordable hatchback that remains one of Latin America's best-selling cars thanks to low running costs and Chevrolet's wide service network. Not exciting, but hard to beat on value for budget-conscious buyers.

models.name: Chevrolet Groove
models.review: A rebadged Wuling Xingchi built for emerging markets, offering solid value and decent fuel economy for a subcompact crossover. The RS turbo trim's 150 hp adds welcome punch over the base engine, making it a sensible budget pick in the Middle East, Latin America, and the Philippines.

models.name: Hyundai Ioniq 5
models.power: 168 kW (229 hp) - Long Range RWD trim
models.review: A practical EV with solid range and ultra-fast charging thanks to its 800V architecture. A smart choice for buyers moving to electric on a mid-range budget, with generous interior space.

models.name: Hyundai Ioniq 6
models.power: 168 kW (225 hp) - Long Range RWD trim
models.range: up to 361 miles (EPA, Long Range RWD)
models.review: A sleek, aerodynamic electric sedan sharing its excellent 800V fast-charging platform with the Ioniq 5 while stretching range further. A strong choice for buyers who want efficiency and a more traditional sedan silhouette.

models.name: Hyundai Tucson
models.review: One of the quickest-accelerating hybrids in its class thanks to the turbocharged hybrid system, backed by Hyundai's outstanding warranty. A smart pick for buyers who want performance and peace of mind together.

models.name: Hyundai Santa Fe
models.review: A boldly styled three-row family SUV where the hybrid trades a bit of acceleration for a big jump in fuel economy. Backed by Hyundai's industry-leading warranty, it's a compelling value against pricier rivals.

models.name: Hyundai Elantra
models.review: An affordable, fuel-efficient compact sedan that also offers a genuinely thrilling N Line and N performance variant for enthusiasts. Excellent value across the whole range, backed by Hyundai's strong warranty.

models.name: Hyundai Sonata
models.review: A stylish midsize sedan where the hybrid trim delivers class-leading fuel economy backed by Hyundai's outstanding warranty coverage. A genuinely compelling alternative to the Camry and Accord hybrids for value-focused buyers.

models.name: Hyundai Kona
models.power: 142 kW (190 hp) - N Line/Limited turbo trim
models.review: A practical subcompact SUV where the turbo engine on N Line and Limited trims adds real pep over the base 147-hp version. The base engine is fine for city driving, but the turbo is worth the upgrade for anyone wanting more confident merging and passing.

models.name: Hyundai Palisade
models.review: A spacious, upscale three-row SUV where the standard V6 delivers smooth, adequate power, with a new turbo hybrid option adding 329 combined horsepower and better efficiency from the 2026 model year. A strong family choice backed by Hyundai's exceptional warranty.

models.name: Hyundai Venue
models.review: Hyundai's most affordable SUV trades outright pace for excellent fuel economy and easy city maneuverability. A sensible pick for budget-conscious first-time buyers who prioritize value and Hyundai's warranty over performance.

models.name: Hyundai Accent
models.review: A budget-friendly, fuel-efficient subcompact that Hyundai has since discontinued in North America in favor of the Venue. A solid, no-frills choice for buyers prioritizing low running costs over features, though it lacks modern active safety tech.

models.name: Hyundai Accent Hatchback
models.review: A budget-friendly, fuel-efficient subcompact that Hyundai has since discontinued in North America in favor of the Venue. A solid, no-frills choice for buyers prioritizing low running costs over features, though it lacks modern active safety tech.

models.name: Kia EV6
models.review: A boldly styled EV with ultra-fast charging, rivaling the Ioniq 5 with similar and sometimes better specs in the sporty GT trim. A strong pick for buyers wanting an electric car with real personality.

models.name: Kia EV9
models.review: A genuinely spacious three-row electric SUV that brings 800V fast-charging to family buyers. A compelling alternative to gas-powered three-rows for those ready to go fully electric, with the GT-Line trim adding real punch.

models.name: Kia Sportage
models.review: Shares its excellent hybrid powertrain with the Tucson but wraps it in bolder styling. Best-in-class power output for the segment makes it a strong value pick for buyers cross-shopping hybrid SUVs.

models.name: Kia Sorento
models.review: A three-row hybrid SUV that trades a little efficiency for stronger acceleration than its Hyundai Santa Fe sibling. Great middle-ground choice for families who want power and space without going full-size.

models.name: Kia Telluride
models.review: A three-row SUV that punches above its price with genuinely upscale interior quality and strong V6 power. One of the best all-rounders in its segment, though it trails hybrid rivals on fuel economy until the next generation arrives.

models.name: Kia Seltos
models.review: A genuinely fun-to-drive subcompact SUV, especially since the 2024 refresh added more power and a smoother 8-speed automatic to the turbo trims. The base 146-hp engine is adequate for city driving, but the turbo is worth seeking out for confident highway merging.

models.name: Kia Soul
models.review: A boxy, characterful subcompact SUV that stays true to its playful design roots while offering above-average fuel economy. The lone naturally aspirated engine is adequate around town, though the previously available turbo would be missed by anyone wanting extra punch.

models.name: Kia K5
models.review: A sharp-looking midsize sedan where the GT-Line's turbo engine offers a nice balance of efficiency and pep, while the range-topping GT's 290-hp 2.5L turbo brings genuine performance-sedan thrills. A stylish alternative to the Camry and Accord for buyers wanting something different.

models.name: Kia Carnival
models.review: One of the most powerful minivans on sale, with a smooth V6 that outguns the Sienna and Odyssey on paper while staying genuinely comfortable to drive. A strong choice for larger families, though all-wheel drive isn't offered.

models.name: Kia Niro
models.review: A class-leading fuel-efficient hybrid crossover offered alongside plug-in hybrid and full-electric versions on the same platform. Not quick, but genuinely practical and cheap to run, with the PHEV adding a noticeably peppier feel for those wanting more oomph.

models.name: Toyota Corolla
models.review: A historically reliable, fuel-efficient compact sedan with low ownership costs. Performance is modest, but it remains the safest bet for buyers prioritizing long-term dependability.

models.name: Toyota Corolla Hatchback
models.review: A historically reliable, fuel-efficient compact sedan with low ownership costs. Performance is modest, but it remains the safest bet for buyers prioritizing long-term dependability.

models.name: Toyota Camry
models.power: 168 kW (225 hp) - Standard Hybrid FWD trim
models.review: The best-selling midsize sedan goes hybrid-exclusive, delivering exceptional fuel economy without giving up the reliability Toyota is famous for. Nearly unbeatable for buyers who want a low-drama, low-cost-to-own daily driver.

models.name: Toyota RAV4
models.power: 169 kW (226 hp) - Standard Hybrid FWD trim
models.review: The best-selling SUV in America goes hybrid-only for this generation, delivering more power and much better fuel economy than before. An outstanding all-rounder for families who want Toyota's legendary reliability without sacrificing efficiency.

models.name: Toyota Land Cruiser
models.fuelConsumption: 22 mpg city / 25 mpg highway (23 mpg combined)
models.review: The legendary off-roader returns to the US with a turbo-hybrid four-cylinder replacing the old V8, delivering far better efficiency without sacrificing genuine off-road capability. A more efficient, tech-laden take on Toyota's rugged icon, though real-world fuel economy runs below the EPA estimate.

models.name: Toyota Yaris
models.power: 70 kW (94 hp) combined - 2024 facelift Hybrid 130 trim
models.review: A remarkably efficient European supermini where the 2024 facelift's more powerful hybrid system makes it genuinely quick off the line despite its small size. A sensible, dependable choice for city driving, though the CVT can get vocal under hard acceleration.

models.name: Toyota Prius
models.review: A dramatically redesigned fifth generation that finally makes the Prius genuinely quick alongside its class-leading fuel economy. A remarkable turnaround for a car once known purely for frugality, and now a legitimately appealing hybrid hatchback.

models.name: Toyota C-HR
models.review: A funky, coupe-styled crossover where the punchier 2.0L Hybrid trim gives genuinely brisk performance, while the base 1.8L version prioritizes efficiency. A stylish alternative to the RAV4 for buyers who don't need three rows or maximum practicality.

models.name: Toyota Highlander
models.review: A dependable three-row family SUV where the hybrid is barely slower than the gas version while using far less fuel. A safe, sensible choice for families who prioritize reliability and resale value over outright excitement.

models.name: Toyota Sienna
models.review: The only hybrid-only minivan on sale, delivering exceptional fuel economy for the segment though acceleration is noticeably more leisurely than V6-powered rivals. A great choice for families prioritizing running costs over outright pace, with a genuinely spacious, well-equipped cabin.

models.name: Toyota Crown
models.power: 176 kW (236 hp) - base Hybrid AWD trim
models.review: A striking, crossover-inspired sedan that fills the gap between mainstream Camry and luxury Lexus. The efficient base hybrid or punchy Hybrid Max give buyers a genuine choice between economy and performance.

models.name: Honda Civic Sedan
models.review: A compact sedan known for reliability and fuel efficiency. Slightly better to drive than the Corolla, and holds its resale value well.

models.name: Honda Civic Hatchback
models.review: A compact sedan known for reliability and fuel efficiency. Slightly better to drive than the Corolla, and holds its resale value well.

models.name: Honda Accord
models.review: Honda's hybrid system out-accelerates most rivals in its class while also topping the fuel economy charts. A genuinely excellent all-rounder for buyers cross-shopping the Camry and Sonata.

models.name: Honda CR-V
models.review: A refined, reliable compact SUV where the hybrid version genuinely elevates the driving experience over the standard gas model. A safe, well-rounded choice that holds strong resale value.

models.name: Honda HR-V
models.review: A subcompact SUV that trades outright pace for genuine Honda reliability and class-leading fuel economy. Not quick, but the composed ride and spacious cabin make it a sensible pick for buyers who prioritize comfort and low running costs over acceleration.

models.name: Honda Pilot
models.review: A rugged-looking, spacious three-row SUV with a genuinely reliable naturally aspirated V6 instead of a turbo. A solid choice for families who value Honda's dependability, though fuel economy trails hybrid rivals.

models.name: Honda Odyssey
models.review: A genuinely engaging minivan to drive thanks to its punchy V6 and slick 10-speed automatic, though fuel economy trails the hybrid-only Sienna. A great pick for families who value driving enjoyment and Honda's reliability over maximum efficiency.

models.name: Honda Passport
models.review: A genuinely quick two-row midsize SUV, among the fastest in its class thanks to its punchy V6, with standard AWD and real off-road capability on the TrailSport trim. Great for buyers who want adventure-ready toughness without a third row, though fuel economy trails rivals.

models.name: Honda Fit
models.power: 92 kW (124 hp) - 1.5L base trim (China/global market, sold as Jazz elsewhere)
models.review: A genuinely spacious and versatile subcompact hatchback, prized for its clever Magic Seat system that maximizes cargo flexibility. Sold as the Jazz in many markets and no longer offered in North America, it remains a smart, efficient choice where it's still available.

models.name: Honda Prologue
models.review: Honda's first mass-market EV shares its GM-derived Ultium platform with the Chevy Blazer EV and Cadillac Lyriq, offering solid range and Honda's familiar interior ergonomics. Reviewers find the driving experience competent but unexciting compared to rivals, with visibility hampered by thick rear pillars.

models.name: Honda ZR-V
models.review: A Civic-based crossover that borrows Honda's excellent hybrid powertrain for genuinely low running costs. A strong, refined alternative to the HR-V for buyers wanting more space and a more premium feel.

models.name: Nissan X-Trail
models.review: A family SUV with the unique e-Power system that delivers an EV-like driving feel without range anxiety. Great for families wanting an electric driving experience without hunting for chargers.

models.name: Nissan Qashqai
models.review: A comfortable, easy-to-drive family crossover with a mild-hybrid engine that keeps fuel bills reasonable. The e-Power hybrid variant is worth the upgrade for buyers wanting a smoother, EV-like driving feel.

models.name: Nissan Altima
models.review: A comfortable, fuel-efficient midsize sedan whose base engine trades outright pace for solid mpg, while the SR VC-Turbo trim adds genuine punch for buyers wanting more excitement. A sensible choice against the Camry and Accord, especially with the excellent highway fuel economy.

models.name: Nissan Sentra
models.review: A no-nonsense, affordably priced compact sedan with solid fuel economy and Nissan's dependable reputation. Not exciting to drive, but a sensible choice for budget-conscious buyers who just want reliable transportation.

models.name: Nissan Pathfinder
models.review: A genuinely capable three-row SUV that's quicker off the line than most rivals like the Highlander and Telluride, backed by a strong towing capacity. A solid family choice, though the V6 can feel rough at idle and fuel economy is unremarkable.

models.name: Nissan Murano
models.review: A stylish two-row midsize SUV with a smooth ride and adequate V6 power, though rivals with turbo fours offer more output from smaller engines. A comfortable, reliable choice for buyers who prioritize a relaxed ride over outright driving thrills.

models.name: Nissan Ariya
models.power: 160 kW (214 hp) - base Engage FWD trim
models.review: A stylish, well-appointed electric SUV whose range varies widely by trim, with the top e-4ORCE dual-motor versions delivering genuinely quick acceleration. Efficiency trails some rivals like the ID.4, but the large battery options help keep real-world range competitive.

models.name: Nissan Leaf
models.review: A dramatic overhaul from the outdated previous generation, with a much bigger battery, genuinely competitive range, and a modern NACS charging port. A significant step forward that finally makes the Leaf a serious rival to the Bolt and Kona Electric again.

models.name: Nissan Kicks
models.review: A genuinely redesigned second generation that finally addresses the old model's biggest weakness by adding both more power and an available AWD option. Still not quick, but a meaningful step up in capability for a subcompact SUV that's easy to park and cheap to run.

models.name: Nissan Juke
models.review: A quirky-styled subcompact crossover where the hybrid trim adds meaningful fuel savings over the standard petrol. Best suited to buyers who want personality and city-friendly size over outright practicality.

models.name: BYD Seal
models.review: A Chinese electric sedan rivaling the Tesla Model 3 with more power at a lower price, backed by BYD's safe Blade battery. Outstanding value for money, though the service network is currently less widespread than Tesla's.

models.name: BYD Atto 3
models.review: A well-equipped electric SUV built around BYD's safe Blade LFP battery, offering competitive range against pricier rivals like the Kona Electric. A strong value proposition for buyers new to EVs, though rear headroom is a bit tight.

models.name: BYD Dolphin
models.review: A compact, affordable electric hatchback that undercuts many established EV rivals on price while offering genuinely usable real-world range on the Extended Range trim. A great entry point for buyers moving to electric on a budget.

models.name: BYD Han
models.review: A genuinely quick flagship EV sedan with supercar-rivalling acceleration in top trim, built on an 800V-capable architecture with fast charging. A serious statement from BYD that undercuts premium European EV sedans on price while matching their performance.

models.name: BYD Tang
models.engineSize: N/A (Full electric) / 1.5L turbo I4 on PHEV variant
models.review: A genuinely quick seven-seat electric SUV flagship, with a huge Blade battery giving strong range for its size and true supercar-level acceleration. A compelling alternative to premium European electric SUVs at a noticeably lower price.

models.name: BYD Song Plus
models.review: One of BYD's best-selling models globally, offering exceptional combined range thanks to its DM-i hybrid system alongside genuinely low running costs. A compelling PHEV alternative to the Qashqai and Tucson, especially for buyers who can charge regularly.

models.name: BYD Seagull
models.review: One of the cheapest EVs on the planet, starting at roughly $10,000 in China, and sold in Europe as the Dolphin Surf. Not quick and best suited to city driving, but a genuinely remarkable price point for a modern electric city car.

models.name: BYD Yuan Plus
models.review: The China-market name for BYD's globally sold Atto 3, sharing identical underpinnings, battery, and motor. A well-rounded, affordable electric SUV that remains one of BYD's best-selling models domestically and abroad.

models.name: BYD Qin Plus
models.review: An exceptionally affordable plug-in hybrid sedan offering a huge combined range on a single tank plus charge. One of BYD's best-selling models thanks to genuinely low running costs, making it a strong budget alternative to compact hybrid sedans.

models.name: Geely Coolray
models.review: A genuinely quick and well-equipped subcompact SUV that punches above its price point, sharing its platform with the Proton X50. A strong value pick for buyers wanting a fun-to-drive crossover without a premium badge.

models.name: Geely Monjaro
models.review: A genuinely upscale-feeling midsize SUV with strong turbo power and standard AWD, offering a lot of equipment for the price. A hybrid version is also available for buyers who want better efficiency without giving up much power.

models.name: Geely Emgrand
models.review: An affordable, no-frills compact sedan that competes on price against the Vios and Mirage G4. Doesn't stand out for driving dynamics, but offers a lot of standard equipment and cabin space for the money.

models.name: Geely Tugella
models.review: A genuinely sporty coupe-SUV built on the Volvo-developed CMA platform, with strong turbo power and standard 4WD for its class. A stylish, performance-oriented alternative for buyers wanting more excitement than a typical crossover.

models.name: Geely Boyue
models.review: One of Geely's best-selling nameplates globally with over 2 million units sold, offering solid space and features for a competitive price. A larger 2.0T option adds real pace for buyers wanting more performance.

models.name: Geely Preface
models.review: A genuinely handsome, well-equipped midsize sedan with a distinctive design and brisk 2.0T performance. A strong value proposition against more established rivals, with a hybrid variant also available for lower running costs.

models.name: Renault Clio
models.power: 116 kW (156 hp) - Full Hybrid E-Tech 160 trim
models.review: A small, highly economical hatchback thanks to its full-hybrid system, with very low emissions and excellent fuel economy. An ideal choice for city driving on a limited budget.

models.name: Renault Megane E-Tech
models.review: A stylish, tech-forward electric hatchback with a slim floor-mounted battery giving it a low center of gravity and genuinely good handling. A strong European alternative to the ID.3 and Kona Electric, especially after the updated model's longer range.

models.name: Renault Captur
models.power: 116 kW (156 hp) - Full Hybrid E-Tech 160 trim
models.review: A stylish subcompact SUV where the E-Tech hybrid delivers genuinely diesel-beating fuel economy without diesel complexity. Strong pick for city and mixed driving with a distinctly French design flair.

models.name: Renault Austral
models.power: 147 kW (200 hp) - E-Tech Full Hybrid 200 trim
models.review: A stylish family SUV where the full-hybrid E-Tech trim delivers genuinely diesel-beating efficiency along with strong torque-rich response. A compelling alternative to the Qashqai and Tucson, with a Formula 1-inspired combustion cycle boosting real-world economy.

models.name: Renault Scenic E-Tech
models.range: 420 km (WLTP, Standard) / over 620 km (WLTP, Long Range)
models.review: A genuinely spacious family electric SUV that returns to the beloved Scenic nameplate, offering strong range on the Long Range trim. A compelling alternative to the ID.4 and Kona Electric for buyers wanting more interior space.

models.name: Renault Arkana
models.power: 105 kW (141-145 hp) - E-Tech Full Hybrid trim
models.review: A distinctively styled coupe-SUV where the full-hybrid system can run in electric mode for up to 80% of city driving time, delivering strong fuel economy. A stylish alternative for buyers wanting a Qashqai-sized SUV with more visual flair.

models.name: Renault Twingo
models.review: The Twingo returns as an all-electric city car built on the same platform as the Renault 5, with a genuinely affordable price point and a first-for-Renault LFP battery. A cheerful, practical alternative to the Dacia Spring and BYD Dolphin Surf for budget-focused urban buyers.

models.name: Renault Symbioz
models.power: 118 kW (158 hp) - E-Tech Full Hybrid 160 trim
models.review: Essentially a longer, more practical estate version of the Captur, with a genuinely bigger boot and Renault's efficient E-Tech hybrid as standard across the range. A sensible family SUV pick, though the Qashqai and Karoq offer sharper handling and more outright cargo space respectively.

models.name: Renault Espace
models.power: 146 kW (196-199 hp) - E-Tech Full Hybrid 200 trim
models.engineSize: 1.2L turbo I3 hybrid + dual electric motors
models.review: The Espace nameplate returns as a hybrid-only SUV rather than a traditional minivan, delivering claimed class-leading efficiency thanks to its sophisticated dual-motor E-Tech system. A genuinely long-legged family hauler, with a claimed combined range approaching 700 miles.

models.name: Renault Rafale
models.co2Emissions: low on PHEV in electric mode
models.review: A striking coupe-SUV flagship that also serves as Renault's answer to the Qashqai-based Rafale, with the top plug-in hybrid AWD trim delivering genuine performance-SUV pace. A stylish, tech-loaded option for buyers wanting more than a standard Austral.

models.name: Renault Logan
models.productionYear: 2021–present (3rd gen, sold in Latin America/Eastern Europe/MENA)
models.review: A famously no-nonsense budget sedan built for durability and low ownership costs over refinement. Hugely popular across Latin America, Eastern Europe, and the Middle East, the Logan remains a go-to choice for buyers who value a spacious, easy-to-maintain car above all else.

models.name: Renault Logan (2017 model, 2nd gen)
models.review: The second-generation Logan that built the nameplate's reputation for tough, low-cost, easy-to-fix motoring across emerging markets. Less refined than the current generation, but a genuinely reliable used-car pick where parts and mechanics are cheap and plentiful.

models.name: Peugeot 208
models.review: A stylish, efficient supermini with mild-hybrid tech that trims fuel use without sacrificing daily usability. Great for city driving and short commutes, though rear space is tight for taller passengers.

models.name: Peugeot 2008
models.review: A stylish subcompact SUV with Peugeot's distinctive i-Cockpit interior, offered alongside a genuinely usable electric e-2008 variant. Efficient and easy to live with, with mild-hybrid versions sharpening both acceleration and fuel economy further.

models.name: Peugeot 3008
models.review: A stylish, tech-forward family SUV where the mild-hybrid trim delivers near-diesel efficiency without diesel complexity. A strong European alternative to the Qashqai and Tucson, with a distinctively futuristic cabin.

models.name: Peugeot 5008
models.review: A genuinely versatile three-row SUV offered across mild-hybrid, plug-in hybrid, and full-electric powertrains, with the electric E-5008 offering strong range up to 410 miles. A rare seven-seat family EV alternative to the Tesla Model Y in Europe.

models.name: Peugeot 308
models.review: A sharp-handling, stylishly designed hatchback where the mild-hybrid system delivers genuinely low emissions and fuel use. A plug-in hybrid and full-electric e-308 are also available for buyers wanting more electrification, all wrapped in Peugeot's distinctive i-Cockpit cabin.

models.name: Peugeot 408
models.review: A striking fastback-crossover that stands out from typical SUV rivals with a genuinely distinctive silhouette. The PHEV trim offers a strong all-electric range for commuting, while a full-electric e-408 rounds out the powertrain lineup.

models.name: Peugeot 508
models.co2Emissions: as low as 29 g/km on PHEV trims
models.review: A sleek executive sedan where the plug-in hybrid delivers genuinely low tailpipe emissions and usable electric-only range, while the flagship PSE HYBRID4 adds true hot-hatch-rivaling acceleration with AWD. A stylish, tech-forward alternative to German rivals.

models.name: Peugeot 4008
models.review: A China-market coupe-SUV nameplate revived by Peugeot's joint venture with Dongfeng, offering distinctive styling and a choice of two turbo engines. Not sold in Europe or North America, it targets buyers in China wanting a sportier alternative to the mainstream 4008's crossover rivals.

models.name: Peugeot 508 SW
models.review: A sleek, low-slung estate that stands out in a market dominated by SUV wagons, sharing its stylish i-Cockpit cabin with the 508 sedan. The base three-cylinder is efficient but modest; the plug-in Hybrid 225 is worth seeking out for buyers wanting genuine daily-electric commuting alongside its estate practicality.

models.name: Volkswagen Golf
models.fuelConsumption: 24 mpg city / 32 mpg highway (27 mpg combined)
models.review: A practical European hatchback with a sporty edge in GTI trim. An excellent balance between fun and daily usability, and strong value within the compact-car segment.

models.name: Volkswagen ID.4
models.power: 210 kW (282 hp) - base Pro RWD trim
models.review: Often called the 'Golf of EVs' for its approachable, no-drama character, the 2026 model simplifies the lineup to a single larger battery for better standard range. The AWD trim's 4.9-second 0-60 time adds genuine pace without sacrificing the ID.4's everyday usability.

models.name: Volkswagen Tiguan
models.review: A composed, well-built compact SUV with German driving manners and a genuinely quick optional engine. Solid choice for buyers who want a more premium feel without stepping up to a luxury badge.

models.name: Volkswagen Passat
models.review: A grown-up, spacious family sedan/wagon that returns to some markets after previously being discontinued. Refined and practical, with a plug-in GTE hybrid option offering genuine daily-commute electric range.

models.name: Volkswagen Polo
models.review: A refined, well-built European supermini that punches above its class in interior quality and driving manners. The GTI variant adds genuine hot-hatch thrills, while the base TSI trims prioritize efficiency for city and commuter driving.

models.name: Volkswagen T-Roc
models.power: 85 kW (116 hp) - 1.5 eTSI base mild-hybrid trim
models.review: A second-generation T-Roc that goes hybrid-only, with a genuinely capable 150hp mild-hybrid option for buyers wanting more pep. The upcoming full-hybrid variants promise even better efficiency, keeping the T-Roc competitive against the Karoq and Qashqai.

models.name: Volkswagen Taos
models.review: A composed, above-average-power subcompact SUV that drives more confidently in corners than most segment rivals. Strong fuel economy and adult-friendly rear seats make it a sensible pick for buyers who want a smaller footprint without feeling underpowered.

models.name: Volkswagen Atlas
models.review: A spacious three-row SUV with a single, adequately powerful turbo-four across the entire lineup, simplifying the buying decision. Genuinely roomy for seven, with a composed ride that suits family road trips better than aggressive off-roading.

models.name: Volkswagen ID.3
models.review: A composed, easy-to-drive electric hatchback that prioritizes everyday usability over outright range or charging speed. The larger 79kWh battery option pushes range past 300 miles for buyers wanting more reassurance on longer trips.

models.name: Volkswagen Touareg
models.review: VW's flagship SUV leans on smooth, torque-rich diesel power for effortless motorway cruising and strong towing capability. A refined, understated alternative to pricier German SUVs, though it's no longer sold in North America.

models.name: BMW 3 Series
models.review: A luxury sports sedan balancing driving enjoyment with everyday comfort. Solid power paired with reasonable fuel efficiency makes it a strong contender in its class, though maintenance costs run higher than Japanese rivals.

models.name: BMW 5 Series
models.review: The benchmark executive sedan, balancing genuine driving engagement with luxury-grade comfort and tech. The base 530i offers strong performance and efficiency, while the 550e plug-in hybrid adds a genuinely usable electric range.

models.name: BMW X3
models.review: A genuinely sporty compact luxury SUV that outguns most rivals on acceleration while staying efficient thanks to its mild-hybrid system. Great for buyers who want driving enjoyment without stepping up to the pricier X5.

models.name: BMW X5
models.review: A well-rounded luxury SUV that balances strong six-cylinder performance with genuine comfort and technology. Excellent for families who want prestige and capability, but fuel economy trails hybrid rivals.

models.name: BMW 1 Series
models.review: BMW's sportiest compact hatchback gains mild-hybrid tech for its fourth generation, with the range-topping M135 xDrive hitting 62 mph in 4.9 seconds. A genuine driver's choice against the Golf and A-Class, prioritizing handling over outright practicality.

models.name: BMW X1
models.review: The entry point into BMW's SUV lineup delivers surprisingly sporty handling for a compact crossover. Great for buyers who want the prestige of the roundel in a smaller, more affordable package.

models.name: BMW 7 Series
models.review: BMW's flagship sedan blends serene comfort with genuine driving engagement, unusual for the segment. The fully electric i7 variants offer a quieter, torque-rich alternative, while the 760i's V8 delivers effortless power for those who want the ultimate in refinement.

models.name: BMW i4
models.review: A genuinely quick, practical electric Gran Coupe that finally gives BMW enthusiasts a proper EV alternative to the 4 Series. The range-topping M60's 593-hp Sport mode makes it one of the quickest BMWs sold today, while the base eDrive40 balances range and performance well.

models.name: BMW iX
models.review: A boldly styled electric SUV that treats performance as a given rather than a premium option, with even the base trim hitting 60 mph in under 5 seconds. The range-topping M70's 650 hp makes it one of the quickest luxury SUVs sold today, electric or otherwise.

models.name: BMW X7
models.review: A three-row luxury SUV that drives with surprising athleticism for its size, even in base trim. The xDrive40i's six-cylinder already feels genuinely quick, making the pricier M60i's extra punch a want rather than a need for most buyers.

models.name: Mercedes-AMG A-Class
models.review: A compact luxury hatchback that balances performance and efficiency thanks to its hybrid system. Great for buyers who want AMG's sporty edge and premium comfort without high fuel costs, though pricing runs higher than segment rivals.

models.name: Mercedes-Benz C-Class
models.review: An accessible entry point into the Mercedes lineup with genuine mild-hybrid efficiency gains and brisk acceleration. Excellent for buyers wanting three-pointed-star prestige with sensible running costs, though options add up quickly.

models.name: Mercedes-Benz E-Class
models.review: A quintessential luxury sedan balancing tech-laden comfort with brisk performance from its base mild-hybrid four-cylinder. The plug-in AMG E53 adds genuine sports-sedan pace, making the E-Class a strong all-rounder across its trim range.

models.name: Mercedes-Benz S-Class
models.review: The flagship of flagship sedans, blending serene comfort with genuinely quick acceleration even in base S500 trim. The S580e plug-in hybrid adds 47+ miles of electric-only range for silent commuting, while remaining the benchmark for luxury-sedan refinement.

models.name: Mercedes-Benz GLC
models.review: One of the best-selling Mercedes models for good reason: refined ride, strong mild-hybrid efficiency, and genuine luxury cabin quality. A benchmark compact luxury SUV, though options can push the price well past rivals.

models.name: Mercedes-Benz GLE
models.review: A versatile midsize luxury SUV offered across six powertrains, from an efficient mild-hybrid four-cylinder to a thundering AMG V8. Strong towing capacity and seven-seat capability make it a genuine family hauler that doesn't skimp on Mercedes refinement.

models.name: Mercedes-Benz GLA
models.review: Mercedes' entry-level SUV brings genuine three-pointed-star prestige to a compact footprint, with the AMG GLA 35 adding real hot-hatch-rivaling pace. A sensible choice for buyers wanting luxury branding without the size or price of the GLC.

models.name: Mercedes-Benz EQS
models.review: Mercedes' electric flagship prioritizes serene, S-Class-rivaling comfort over outright drama, with segment-leading range on the base 450+ trim. The AMG-tuned versions add genuine pace, but most buyers will find the base trim's smooth, quiet character the real draw.

models.name: Mercedes-Benz EQE
models.review: A smaller, more affordable sibling to the EQS that keeps most of the flagship's comfort and tech at a lower price. A solid choice for buyers wanting a Mercedes EV sedan without the S-Class-adjacent price tag, though range trails some rivals.

models.name: Mercedes-Benz CLA
models.power: 200 kW (268 hp) - CLA 250+ Electric base trim
models.review: A completely reinvented CLA launches electric-first with genuinely class-leading range and ultra-fast 800V charging. A gasoline hybrid version arrives later for buyers not ready to go electric, but the EV variant's efficiency and tech make it the star of the new lineup.

models.name: Ferrari Roma
models.review: An elegant grand tourer combining Ferrari's signature V8 punch with everyday usability rarely found in the marque's lineup. A true entry point into Ferrari ownership, though running costs and depreciation remain significant considerations.

models.name: Ferrari 296 GTB
models.power: 610 kW (819 hp combined) - 654 hp V6 + 165 hp electric motor
models.review: A more intimate, engaging alternative to the bigger SF90, with a howling V6 that some enthusiasts prefer over Ferrari's V8s. Genuinely usable as a daily driver in electric mode around town, then devastatingly fast the moment the V6 wakes up.

models.name: Ferrari SF90 Stradale
models.power: 725 kW (986 hp combined) - 769 hp V8 + 217 hp from three electric motors
models.review: Ferrari's first plug-in hybrid remains its most powerful road car, with all-wheel-drive traction from front-mounted electric motors giving genuinely hypercar-rivaling launch performance. A landmark model that proved electrification could make a Ferrari faster, not slower.

models.name: Ferrari Purosangue
models.review: Ferrari's first four-door, four-seat model refuses to call itself an SUV, and drives more like a lifted sports car thanks to its naturally aspirated V12 and low-slung stance. Production is deliberately capped at 20% of Ferrari's output to preserve exclusivity, making it one of the hardest cars on this list to actually buy.

models.name: Ferrari 812 Competizione
models.review: Limited to 999 units, this is widely considered the pinnacle of naturally aspirated V12 engineering and likely Ferrari's last non-hybrid V12 road car. A genuine collector's piece that trades everyday usability for the purest possible expression of Ferrari's front-engine berlinetta formula.

models.name: Fiat 500e
models.review: A charming, compact city EV with genuine Italian style and zero-emission running costs. Perfect for urban dwellers with short commutes, though its limited range makes it unsuitable for long road trips.

models.name: Fiat Panda
models.power: 80 kW (108 hp) - Grande Panda mild-hybrid trim
models.review: The all-new retro-styled Grande Panda brings genuine nostalgic charm and surprising practicality to the city-car segment, now also offered as a full EV with a 199-mile range. The cabin feels a bit low-rent for the segment, but few small cars are this easy to smile about.

models.name: Fiat Tipo Sedan
models.review: An affordable, roomy sedan that competes on value rather than driving excitement, with a spacious trunk that outclasses many segment rivals. A sensible budget choice, particularly in markets where Fiat's dealer network and parts availability are strong.

models.name: Fiat Tipo Hatchback
models.review: A practical, no-frills hatchback offering a genuinely spacious cabin and boot for its class. The efficient 1.6 Multijet diesel is worth considering for high-mileage buyers, returning some of the best fuel economy in the segment.

models.name: Fiat 600e
models.review: A stylish Italian-flavored electric crossover sharing its bones with the Jeep Avenger, offering solid range and fast charging for the class. The hot Abarth 600e version adds genuine hot-hatch power for buyers wanting more excitement.

models.name: Fiat Pulse
models.power: 92 kW (125 hp gasoline / 130 hp ethanol) - 1.0 Turbo T200 trim
models.review: Fiat's first SUV developed entirely in Brazil has become a runaway sales success in Latin America, thanks to flex-fuel versatility and a genuinely punchy turbo option. The mild-hybrid Impetus trim adds a bit more refinement and efficiency for buyers wanting the top of the range.

models.name: Jaguar F-Pace
models.review: A stylish performance SUV that handles like a sports car while offering everyday practicality. The base engine balances efficiency and refinement well, though Jaguar's reduced dealer network may affect long-term ownership convenience.

models.name: Jaguar I-Pace
models.review: One of the first credible luxury EV rivals to Tesla, still delivering genuinely sports-car-like acceleration years after launch. Charging speed and range now trail newer rivals, but the I-Pace remains a distinctive, well-built choice for buyers wanting something different from the German norm.

models.name: Range Rover
models.power: 295 kW (395 hp) - P400 SE base trim
models.review: The original luxury SUV remains the benchmark for effortless off-road capability paired with limousine-grade comfort. The plug-in hybrid P460e offers a genuinely usable 50+ mile electric range, while the range-topping SV brings supercar-adjacent power to a two-and-a-half-ton SUV.

models.name: Range Rover Sport
models.power: 265 kW (355 hp) - P360 SE base trim
models.review: A powerful, road-focused luxury SUV that blends genuine off-road capability with sports-car-like acceleration. A strong all-rounder for buyers who want prestige and performance, but fuel economy and running costs are steep.

models.name: Range Rover Velar
models.review: The design-focused middle child of the Range Rover lineup, prized for its minimalist styling and superb interior. The optional P400 mild-hybrid six-cylinder is worth seeking out for buyers who want more urgency than the adequate but unremarkable base four-cylinder provides.

models.name: Range Rover Evoque
models.review: A stylish, compact luxury SUV that trades some outright pace for genuine off-road ability rare in this segment. A strong choice for buyers wanting Range Rover styling and capability in a smaller, more affordable package.

models.name: Land Rover Discovery
models.power: 221 kW (296 hp) - P300 S base trim
models.review: A genuinely capable three-row family SUV that backs up its off-road credentials with real luxury and seven-seat practicality. The six-cylinder mild-hybrid upgrade adds meaningful towing capacity without hurting efficiency much, making it worth the step up for buyers who tow regularly.

models.name: Land Rover Discovery Sport
models.review: A compact luxury SUV that punches above its class with an optional third row and genuine Terrain Response off-road tech, both rare in this segment. A sensible entry point into Land Rover ownership, though it's beginning to show its age against newer rivals like the BMW X3.

models.name: Land Rover Defender
models.review: A go-anywhere off-roader that doesn't sacrifice on-road comfort or technology, with an engine range spanning efficient four-cylinder to thunderous V8 OCTA. Genuine capability for adventurous buyers, though fuel economy and running costs are steep across the range.

models.name: Mini Cooper
models.review: A go-kart-like hot hatch that stays true to Mini's driving-fun heritage while adding modern tech. Best suited to buyers who prioritize personality and handling over outright practicality.

models.name: Mini Countryman
models.power: 180 kW (241 hp) - S ALL4 base gasoline trim
models.fuelConsumption: 24 mpg city / 32 mpg highway (27 mpg combined)
models.review: Mini's largest model finally gets a proper electric-first launch alongside the familiar turbo-four gasoline version. The JCW trim's 312 hp makes it genuinely quick for a small SUV, while the base S ALL4 balances Mini's go-kart handling character with everyday practicality.

models.name: Mini Aceman
models.power: 135 kW (184 hp) - Aceman E base trim
models.review: Mini's smallest electric crossover blends Cooper-like go-kart handling with genuinely useful extra space over the two-door hatch. Range trails class leaders like the Kia EV3, and the ride can feel firm on the sportier JCW trim, but it remains one of the most fun-to-drive small EVs available.

models.name: Aston Martin Vantage
models.review: A visceral British sports car with AMG-sourced V8 power and true supercar-level acceleration. Best for driving purists who want an emotional, hand-built alternative to Porsche and Ferrari rivals, at a steep running cost.

models.name: Aston Martin DB12
models.review: Aston Martin's self-declared 'Super Tourer' blends genuine supercar-rivaling acceleration with proper long-distance comfort. The new DB12 S pushes power to 690 hp for buyers wanting the sharpest version, but the base car already outguns most direct GT rivals.

models.name: Aston Martin DBX
models.review: The self-proclaimed 'supercar of SUVs' backs up the claim with genuine 3.1-second 0-60 acceleration from its AMG-sourced V8. The new DBX S pushes power to 717 hp for the most power-dense SUV on the planet, though rivals like the Purosangue and Urus give it real competition.

models.name: Aston Martin Vanquish
models.review: Aston Martin's returning flagship packs the most powerful engine the brand has ever built into a genuinely usable grand tourer with a back seat. Limited to 1,000 units a year and starting near $430,000, it's an exclusive alternative to the Ferrari 12Cilindri and Bentley Continental GT Speed.

models.name: Volvo XC60
models.power: 184 kW (247 hp) - B5 mild-hybrid base trim
models.review: A luxury SUV focused on safety and Scandinavian comfort, with a genuinely powerful PHEV version for those wanting performance and efficiency together. Pricing runs high, but the safety and equipment levels justify it.

models.name: Volvo XC90
models.power: 184 kW (247 hp) - B5 mild-hybrid base trim
models.review: A safety-focused three-row family SUV with Scandinavian design and strong mild-hybrid efficiency. Ideal for families prioritizing comfort and crash-test performance over outright speed.

models.name: Volvo XC40
models.review: A stylish, safety-focused compact luxury SUV with genuinely punchy performance in B5 trim. A strong choice for urban families who value Scandinavian design and top-tier crash protection over outright efficiency.

models.name: Volvo EX30
models.power: 200 kW (268 hp) - Single Motor Extended Range trim
models.review: Volvo's smallest, most affordable EV punches well above its price with genuinely quick acceleration and a minimalist, recycled-material-heavy cabin. The Twin Motor Performance trim's 3.4-second 0-60 time makes it the fastest Volvo ever built, remarkable for the brand's entry-level model.

models.name: Volvo EX90
models.power: 245 kW (329 hp) - Single Motor base trim
models.review: Volvo's flagship three-row electric SUV moves to an 800V architecture for 2026, cutting charging times significantly and boosting power across the range. The Twin Motor Performance's 670 hp makes it genuinely quick for a family hauler, though reliability ratings have lagged rivals so far.

models.name: Volvo S60
models.power: 184 kW (247 hp) - B5 base mild-hybrid trim
models.review: A comfortable, safety-focused compact luxury sedan where the plug-in T8 Recharge trim adds genuinely quick performance and up to 41 miles of electric-only range. Handling is more relaxed than German rivals, prioritizing ride comfort over outright sportiness.

models.name: Volvo S90
models.power: 220 kW (295 hp) - B6 base mild-hybrid trim
models.review: A spacious, understated luxury sedan that prioritizes Scandinavian comfort and class-leading safety over sporty handling. The T8 Recharge plug-in hybrid pushes output to 455 hp while adding up to 38 miles of electric range, making it a genuinely versatile flagship.

models.name: Volvo V60
models.power: 184 kW (247 hp) - B5 base mild-hybrid trim
models.review: A rare wagon holdout in a market dominated by SUVs, with the Cross Country trim adding genuine light off-road capability. The Polestar Engineered version's 455-hp plug-in hybrid setup makes it a genuine sleeper for enthusiasts who want cargo space and speed together.

models.name: Volvo V90
models.power: 220 kW (295 hp) - B6 base mild-hybrid trim
models.review: A large, handsome luxury wagon that remains genuinely quick despite its size, with the Cross Country trim adding usable off-road capability. A rare, refined alternative to midsize luxury SUVs for buyers who still want a lower-slung driving position.

models.name: Skoda Octavia
models.review: A highly practical sedan with interior space that outclasses its segment, built on a proven Volkswagen Group platform with solid reliability and a lower price than direct German rivals.

models.name: Skoda Octavia Combi
models.review: A highly practical sedan with interior space that outclasses its segment, built on a proven Volkswagen Group platform with solid reliability and a lower price than direct German rivals.

models.name: Skoda Superb
models.review: A cavernous liftback that punches above its price with genuine luxury-car space and refinement. The range-topping 265hp AWD trim adds surprising pace, making it one of the best value large cars in Europe.

models.name: Skoda Kodiaq
models.power: 110 kW (148 hp) - 1.5 TSI mild-hybrid base trim
models.review: A genuinely spacious seven-seat family SUV that now adds a plug-in hybrid iV variant offering up to 75 miles of electric range. Shares its bones with the VW Tiguan but undercuts it on price while matching its practicality, making it a smart pick for value-focused families.

models.name: Skoda Karoq
models.review: A no-nonsense, right-sized compact SUV that prioritizes practicality and value over flashy tech, with a genuinely spacious cabin for its footprint. A sensible alternative to pricier German rivals for buyers who don't need a hybrid or plug-in powertrain.

models.name: Skoda Fabia
models.review: A genuinely spacious and well-built supermini that punches above its class in interior room, thanks to sharing its platform with the VW Polo. The efficient base 1.0 TSI is well suited to city and commuter driving, with the sportier Monte Carlo trim adding a bit more visual flair.

models.name: Skoda Scala
models.review: A practical, spacious hatchback that prioritizes comfort and boot space over driving thrills, standing out with a bigger cargo hold than most rivals its size. Not the most exciting car to drive, but a sensible, well-priced alternative to the Golf and Focus.

models.name: Skoda Kamiq
models.review: A composed, comfort-focused subcompact SUV that balances agility and ride quality better than most segment rivals. The base 1.0 TSI is fine for city use, but the punchier 1.5 TSI is worth the upgrade for buyers wanting more highway confidence.

models.name: Skoda Enyaq
models.range: 268 miles (WLTP, 60 trim) / up to 359 miles (85 trim)
models.review: A genuinely practical electric SUV offered in both boxy and sleeker Coupe body styles, with the 85 trim's 359-mile range among the best in its class. Charging speed trails 800V rivals like the Ioniq 5, but most owners charging overnight at home won't notice the difference.

models.name: SEAT Leon
models.review: A sharp-handling hatchback that shares its bones with the VW Golf at a friendlier price point. Great value for buyers who want German-platform engineering with a sportier, younger image.

models.name: SEAT Ibiza
models.review: A sharp-handling supermini that shares its bones with the Ibiza's Skoda and VW cousins but wears more youthful, sporty styling. The 1.0 TSI 95 is the sweet spot in the range, delivering confident performance and genuinely good real-world fuel economy.

models.name: SEAT Arona
models.review: A jacked-up Ibiza in all but name, offering a slightly higher driving position and a bit more visual crossover appeal in a genuinely fun-to-drive package. The 115hp engine is the sweet spot in the range, striking the right balance of punch and efficiency.

models.name: SEAT Ateca
models.review: A genuinely fun-to-drive family SUV that undercuts pricier rivals like the Tiguan and 3008 while sharing much of their underlying engineering. The 1.5-liter engine is the pick of the range for most buyers, striking a nice balance of pep and efficiency.

models.name: SEAT Tarraco
models.review: SEAT's largest, most practical SUV shares its bones with the Skoda Kodiaq and VW Tiguan Allspace, offering genuine seven-seat family space at a friendlier price. The diesel is worth considering for high-mileage drivers, delivering over 50 mpg on official tests.
